claim: Δ13C values were significantly higher in rainforest than in the other land-use systems in Coleoptera, Diplopoda, Hemiptera, Orthoptera, Pauropoda, Protura, Pseudoscorpiones, and Thysanoptera.
source: The Δ13C values were significantly higher in rainforest than in the other land-use systems in Coleoptera, Diplopoda, Hemiptera, Orthoptera, Pauropoda, Protura, Pseudoscorpiones, and Thysanoptera (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis of stable isotope data, with reference to Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most groups in rainforest were higher in Δ13C by 1–3‰ than in the other land-use systems.
source: In general, most groups in rainforest were higher in Δ13C by 1–3‰ than in the other land-use systems, but this shift was only significant for two out of six macrodecomposer groups.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's stable isotope analysis.

claim: Annelida had similar Δ13C values across land-use systems.
source: Annelida, which accounted for much of the community metabolism in each of the land-use systems, had similar Δ13C values across land-use systems.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's stable isotope analysis.

claim: Δ15N values of Oribatida and Blattodea were by 1.5–2.5‰ lower in rainforest than in the other land-use systems.
source: The Δ15N values were by 1.5–2.5‰ lower in rainforest than in the other land-use systems in Oribatida and Blattodea (except for similar Δ15N values in oil palm and rainforest for Blattodea).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's stable isotope analysis.

claim: Δ15N values of Hemiptera, Orthoptera, Isoptera, and Pseudoscorpiones were lower in oil palm than in rainforest.
source: By contrast, Δ15N values of Hemiptera, Orthoptera, Isoptera, and Pseudoscorpiones were lower in oil palm than in rainforest, whereas in jungle rubber this was only true for Orthoptera (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's stable isotope analysis, with reference to Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The maxima of Δ13C values were by 1–2‰ higher in forest than in jungle rubber and oil palm plantations.
source: The maxima of Δ13C values were by 1–2‰ higher in forest than in jungle rubber and oil palm plantations, but minima and the overall range did not differ significantly (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of one-dimensional isotopic metrics, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The unweighted average Δ13C values of communities were by 1–2‰ higher in rainforest than in the other land-use systems.
source: The unweighted average Δ13C values of communities were by 1–2‰ higher in rainforest than in the other land-use systems and were also higher in rubber than in oil palm plantations.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of one-dimensional isotopic metrics.

claim: The energetic average positions of Δ13C did not differ significantly across land-use systems.
source: However, the energetic average positions did not differ significantly due to similar Δ13C values of Annelida (dominant invertebrate group) across land-use systems (Figure 2e, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of one-dimensional isotopic metrics, with reference to Figure 2e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Jungle rubber had the largest range in Δ15N values (16.5‰) among the four land-use systems.
source: Extreme values of Δ15N were most pronounced in jungle rubber, both maximum and minimum, resulting in the largest range in Δ15N values (16.5‰) among the four land-use systems.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of one-dimensional isotopic metrics.

claim: The unweighted average Δ15N values of communities were lowest in oil palm.
source: The unweighted average Δ15N values of communities were lowest in oil palm, being significantly lower than in rubber (Figure 3i).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of one-dimensional isotopic metrics, with reference to Figure 3i.

claim: The energetic average Δ15N values did not differ significantly across land-use systems.
source: By contrast, the energetic average Δ15N values did not differ significantly.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of one-dimensional isotopic metrics.

claim: Isotopic dispersion was significantly higher in oil palm than in each of the other land-use systems (community metrics).
source: Among the unweighted metrics (i.e., community metrics), isotopic dispersion was significantly higher in oil palm than in each of the other land-use systems; isotopic divergence and uniqueness were significantly higher in oil palm than in jungle rubber; isotopic evenness was significantly lower in jungle rubber than in each of the other land-use systems; only isotopic richness showed no significant differences between land-use systems, but in trend the two monoculture systems had lower values than in rainforest and jungle rubber.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of multidimensional isotopic metrics.

claim: Isotopic divergence and uniqueness were significantly higher in oil palm than in jungle rubber (community metrics).
source: Among the unweighted metrics (i.e., community metrics), isotopic dispersion was significantly higher in oil palm than in each of the other land-use systems; isotopic divergence and uniqueness were significantly higher in oil palm than in jungle rubber; isotopic evenness was significantly lower in jungle rubber than in each of the other land-use systems; only isotopic richness showed no significant differences between land-use systems, but in trend the two monoculture systems had lower values than in rainforest and jungle rubber.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of multidimensional isotopic metrics.

claim: Isotopic evenness was significantly lower in jungle rubber than in each of the other land-use systems (community metrics).
source: Among the unweighted metrics (i.e., community metrics), isotopic dispersion was significantly higher in oil palm than in each of the other land-use systems; isotopic divergence and uniqueness were significantly higher in oil palm than in jungle rubber; isotopic evenness was significantly lower in jungle rubber than in each of the other land-use systems; only isotopic richness showed no significant differences between land-use systems, but in trend the two monoculture systems had lower values than in rainforest and jungle rubber.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of multidimensional isotopic metrics.

claim: Isotopic richness showed no significant differences between land-use systems (community metrics).
source: Among the unweighted metrics (i.e., community metrics), isotopic dispersion was significantly higher in oil palm than in each of the other land-use systems; isotopic divergence and uniqueness were significantly higher in oil palm than in jungle rubber; isotopic evenness was significantly lower in jungle rubber than in each of the other land-use systems; only isotopic richness showed no significant differences between land-use systems, but in trend the two monoculture systems had lower values than in rainforest and jungle rubber.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of multidimensional isotopic metrics.

claim: The weighted multidimensional metrics (energetic metrics) did not differ among land-use systems for isotopic dispersion, isotopic evenness, isotopic richness, and isotopic uniqueness.
source: By contrast, the weighted multidimensional metrics (i.e., energetic metrics) did not differ among land-use systems for isotopic dispersion, isotopic evenness, isotopic richness, and isotopic uniqueness (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of multidimensional isotopic metrics, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Isotopic divergence was significantly lower in rainforest than in the other land-use systems (energetic metrics).
source: Only isotopic divergence was significantly lower in rainforest than in the other land-use systems, showing an opposite trend to isotopic dispersion.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of multidimensional isotopic metrics.

claim: Community metrics differed strongly between the four land-use systems (anosim R = 0.404, p < 0.001).
source: As indicated by multivariate analysis, community metrics differed strongly between the four land-use systems (anosim R = 0.404, p < 0.001), whereas differences for the energetic metrics were less pronounced (anosim R = 0.138, p = 0.014).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's multivariate statistical analysis.

claim: Differences for the energetic metrics were less pronounced (anosim R = 0.138, p = 0.014).
source: As indicated by multivariate analysis, community metrics differed strongly between the four land-use systems (anosim R = 0.404, p < 0.001), whereas differences for the energetic metrics were less pronounced (anosim R = 0.138, p = 0.014).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's multivariate statistical analysis.

claim: Soil pH, tree species richness, litter amount, and understory density had the strongest correlations with both community metrics and energetic metrics.
source: Among all tested environmental factors, soil pH, tree species richness, litter amount, and understory density had the strongest correlations with both community metrics (p = 0.003, p = 0.037, p < 0.001, p < 0.001, respectively) and energetic metrics (p = 0.004, p = 0.002, p = 0.003, p = 0.002, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's correlation analysis.

claim: Changes in the community metrics (PC1unweighted) were induced directly by tree properties and litter amount.
source: SEM indicated that the changes in the community metrics (PC1unweighted) were induced directly by tree properties and litter amount (tree density: p < 0.05, effect size = 0.72; tree species richness: p < 0.001, effect size = –0.83; litter amount: p < 0.001, effect size = 0.71), while changes in the energetic metrics (PC1weighted) were indirectly driven by soil pH via increased metabolism of earthworms (p < 0.05, effect size = –0.36; Figure 5; Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's structural equation modeling, with reference to Figure 5 and Figure 6.

claim: Changes in the energetic metrics (PC1weighted) were indirectly driven by soil pH via increased metabolism of earthworms.
source: SEM indicated that the changes in the community metrics (PC1unweighted) were induced directly by tree properties and litter amount (tree density: p < 0.05, effect size = 0.72; tree species richness: p < 0.001, effect size = –0.83; litter amount: p < 0.001, effect size = 0.71), while changes in the energetic metrics (PC1weighted) were indirectly driven by soil pH via increased metabolism of earthworms (p < 0.05, effect size = –0.36; Figure 5; Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's structural equation modeling, with reference to Figure 5 and Figure 6.

claim: Collembola, Symphyla, and Isopoda showed a much higher 15N enrichment than Oribatida in tropical forests.
source: Collembola, Symphyla, and Isopoda showed a much higher 15N enrichment than, for example, Oribatida, but all three groups occupy similar trophic positions in temperate forests and predominantly function as decomposers (Potapov et al., 2019c).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's stable isotope analysis, compared with cited research on temperate forests.

claim: The higher 15N enrichment in Collembola, Symphyla, and Isopoda may be caused by low litter quality in tropical forests forcing decomposers to switch to more microbial or even animal diet.
source: This difference may be caused by low litter quality in tropical forests forcing decomposers to switch to more microbial or even animal diet (Illig et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data, supported by a citation.

claim: Protura in temperate forests are enriched in 15N and feed on ectomycorrhizal fungi.
source: Protura in temperate forests are enriched in 15N and feed on ectomycorrhizal fungi (Bluhm et al., 2019), whereas in the studied tropical forests, Protura had the lowest Δ15N values among all groups, suggesting that they feed on saprotrophic rather than mycorrhizal fungi.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In the studied tropical forests, Protura had the lowest Δ15N values among all groups, suggesting that they feed on saprotrophic rather than mycorrhizal fungi.
source: Protura in temperate forests are enriched in 15N and feed on ectomycorrhizal fungi (Bluhm et al., 2019), whereas in the studied tropical forests, Protura had the lowest Δ15N values among all groups, suggesting that they feed on saprotrophic rather than mycorrhizal fungi.
evidence: This is a finding and interpretation from the study's stable isotope analysis.

claim: The low Δ15N and high Δ13C values of Pauropoda indicate that they function as decomposers by feeding on saprotrophic microorganisms.
source: The low Δ15N and high Δ13C values of Pauropoda, reported for the first time for this group, indicate that they function as decomposers by feeding on saprotrophic microorganisms (Tiunov et al., 2015), confirming earlier suggestions (Starling, 1944).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's stable isotope data, supported by citations.

claim: Low Δ15N values in Protura, Diplopoda, Isoptera, Psocoptera, and Blattodea may be associated with feeding on algae.
source: Low Δ15N values in Protura, Diplopoda, Isoptera, Psocoptera, and Blattodea may be associated with feeding on algae (Potapov et al., 2018), shown to be important food for mesofauna in tropical soil food webs (Susanti et al., 2019; Semenina et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data, supported by citations.

claim: Micropredators had higher trophic positions (Δ15N values) than macropredators across all land-use systems.
source: Unexpectedly, micropredators (e.g., Diplura and Pseudoscorpiones) had higher trophic positions (Δ15N values) than macropredators (e.g., Araneae and Formicidae) across all land-use systems, and Diplura had the highest Δ15N values among all taxa studied.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's stable isotope analysis.

claim: The higher trophic position of small-sized predators suggests that they form part of a different energy channel than macropredators.
source: The higher trophic position of small-sized predators suggests that they form part of a different energy channel than macropredators.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's stable isotope data.

claim: The micro-food web in soil is based mainly on microbial resources channeled to higher trophic levels by microarthropod predators.
source: In fact, the micro-food web in soil has been shown to be based mainly on microbial resources channeled to higher trophic levels by microarthropod predators, whereas the macro-food web is based more on litter and detritus consumed by macrofauna taxa with the energy channeled to higher trophic levels by macroarthropod predators (Potapov et al., 2021a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The macro-food web is based more on litter and detritus consumed by macrofauna taxa with the energy channeled to higher trophic levels by macroarthropod predators.
source: In fact, the micro-food web in soil has been shown to be based mainly on microbial resources channeled to higher trophic levels by microarthropod predators, whereas the macro-food web is based more on litter and detritus consumed by macrofauna taxa with the energy channeled to higher trophic levels by macroarthropod predators (Potapov et al., 2021a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The micro-food web has more trophic transactions than the macro-food web, explaining the higher trophic position of micro- than macroarthropod predators.
source: This implies more trophic transactions in the micro-food web (Pollierer et al., 2009; Steffan et al., 2015) explaining the higher trophic position of micro- than macroarthropod predators.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's data and cited research.

claim: Diptera had higher isotopic values (both Δ15N and Δ13C) than Coleoptera.
source: Among other groups with a wide food spectrum, Diptera had higher isotopic values (both Δ15N and Δ13C) than Coleoptera, indicating that flies are more closely linked to detrital and microbial food chains in tropical soil food webs than beetles.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's stable isotope analysis.

claim: Flies are more closely linked to detrital and microbial food chains in tropical soil food webs than beetles.
source: Among other groups with a wide food spectrum, Diptera had higher isotopic values (both Δ15N and Δ13C) than Coleoptera, indicating that flies are more closely linked to detrital and microbial food chains in tropical soil food webs than beetles.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's stable isotope data.

claim: Isopoda had strikingly high Δ15N values for macrodecomposers, possibly due to intense coprophagy.
source: Isopoda had strikingly high Δ15N values for macrodecomposers, possibly due to intense coprophagy (Potapov et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a finding and speculative interpretation from the study's stable isotope analysis, supported by a citation.

claim: There are consistent differences between tropical and temperate soil food webs.
source: Overall, despite general similarities, we also found consistent differences between tropical and temperate soil food webs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings compared with knowledge of temperate systems.

claim: The 13C concentration in dead plant material is increasing during decomposition compared to fresh leaf litter.
source: The 13C concentration in dead plant material is increasing during decomposition compared to fresh leaf litter (Ågren et al., 1996; Boström et al., 2007; Potapov et al., 2019c), and high Δ13C values in soil fauna in forest likely indicate feeding on saprotrophic fungi and bacteria that assimilate predominantly labile 13C-enriched plant compounds (Pollierer et al., 2009; Potapov et al., 2013; Hyodo, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: High Δ13C values in soil fauna in forest likely indicate feeding on saprotrophic fungi and bacteria that assimilate predominantly labile 13C-enriched plant compounds.
source: The 13C concentration in dead plant material is increasing during decomposition compared to fresh leaf litter (Ågren et al., 1996; Boström et al., 2007; Potapov et al., 2019c), and high Δ13C values in soil fauna in forest likely indicate feeding on saprotrophic fungi and bacteria that assimilate predominantly labile 13C-enriched plant compounds (Pollierer et al., 2009; Potapov et al., 2013; Hyodo, 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the study's data and cited research.

claim: Vascular and non-vascular plants have generally lower Δ13C values than saprotrophic microorganisms and animals.
source: Vascular and non-vascular plants have generally lower Δ13C values than saprotrophic microorganisms and animals (Hyodo et al., 2010; Potapov et al., 2019c), therefore, the high Δ13C values in soil invertebrates in rainforest point to a more pronounced detritus-based 'brown' food web relying heavily on saprotrophic fungi and bacteria based on litter material.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The high Δ13C values in soil invertebrates in rainforest point to a more pronounced detritus-based 'brown' food web relying heavily on saprotrophic fungi and bacteria based on litter material.
source: Vascular and non-vascular plants have generally lower Δ13C values than saprotrophic microorganisms and animals (Hyodo et al., 2010; Potapov et al., 2019c), therefore, the high Δ13C values in soil invertebrates in rainforest point to a more pronounced detritus-based 'brown' food web relying heavily on saprotrophic fungi and bacteria based on litter material.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the study's data and cited research.

claim: The unweighted average Δ13C values were lowest in oil palm suggesting a shift toward a more plant-based 'green' food web.
source: Among the plantations, the unweighted average Δ13C values were lowest in oil palm suggesting a shift toward a more plant-based 'green' food web relying more heavily on the consumption of living plant tissue (Fujii et al., 2021), which has been previously shown for Chilopoda, Oribatida, Collembola, and Pseudoscorpiones at the same study sites (Klarner et al., 2017; Krause et al., 2019; Liebke et al., 2021; Susanti et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's data, supported by citations to previous research at the same sites.

claim: The herb layer is much more developed in plantations due to more open canopy and coverage by weeds.
source: Compared to rainforest the herb layer is much more developed in plantations due to more open canopy and coverage by weeds (Rembold et al., 2017a), presumably providing high-quality resources for plant and litter feeding soil animals.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Litter in rainforest is high in lignin and therefore of low food quality.
source: By contrast, litter in rainforest is high in lignin and therefore of low food quality (Krashevska et al., 2018), increasing the use of saprotrophic microorganisms rather than litter by detritivores (Illig et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The bacterial energy channel typically is considered to be 'fast', while the fungal energy channel is considered to be 'slow'.
source: In soil food-web models the bacterial energy channel typically is considered to be 'fast', while the fungal energy channel is considered to be 'slow' due to differences in the turnover rates of bacteria and their consumers, and fungi and their consumers, respectively (Coleman et al., 1983; Moore et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research and represents established knowledge in soil ecology.

claim: The fast energy channel is defined by fast-growing populations with short turnover rates.
source: Generally, the fast energy channel is defined by fast-growing populations with short turnover rates (Rooney et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Animals feeding on living plants or fresh litter contribute to fast energy channeling, whereas animals feeding on recalcitrant detritus are associated with slow energy channeling.
source: Based on this concept, animals feeding on living plants or fresh litter contribute to fast energy channeling, whereas animals feeding on recalcitrant detritus (being slowly decomposed belowground) are associated with slow energy channeling.
evidence: This is an application of established concepts to the study's context.

claim: 13C accumulates in plant-derived materials with microbial decomposition.
source: Since 13C accumulates in plant-derived materials with microbial decomposition (Pollierer et al., 2009; Potapov et al., 2013; Fujii et al., 2021), Δ13C values in soil animals may indicate slow versus fast carbon cycling in soil.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Δ13C values in soil animals may indicate slow versus fast carbon cycling in soil.
source: Since 13C accumulates in plant-derived materials with microbial decomposition (Pollierer et al., 2009; Potapov et al., 2013; Fujii et al., 2021), Δ13C values in soil animals may indicate slow versus fast carbon cycling in soil.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited research and the study's data.

claim: The shift toward plant-based energy channeling in food webs of plantations may reflect accelerated carbon cycling at the ecosystem level.
source: Therefore, the shift toward plant-based energy channeling in food webs of plantations may reflect accelerated carbon cycling at the ecosystem level, contributing to carbon losses of plantations (Guillaume et al., 2018) and thereby potentially compromising ecosystem long-term stability (McCann et al., 1998; Rooney and McCann, 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings, supported by citations.

claim: Earthworms feed on detritus and microorganisms and are able to efficiently use fresh litter carbon, but also 'old' microbially processed carbon.
source: Earthworms feed on detritus and microorganisms and are able to efficiently use fresh litter carbon, but also 'old' microbially processed carbon (e.g., soil organic matter; Scheu and Falca, 2000; Hyodo et al., 2012; Blouin et al., 2013) reflected in high Δ13C values (Pollierer et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Land-use change in tropical lowland landscapes is associated with the loss of biodiversity and reduced biomass of litter arthropods.
source: Land-use change in tropical lowland landscapes is associated with the loss of biodiversity and reduced biomass of litter arthropods (Barnes et al., 2014), but the negative effect of biodiversity loss on soil functions may be at least in part counteracted by earthworms that monopolize the detrital channel in plantations.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The negative effect of biodiversity loss on soil functions may be at least in part counteracted by earthworms that monopolize the detrital channel in plantations.
source: Land-use change in tropical lowland landscapes is associated with the loss of biodiversity and reduced biomass of litter arthropods (Barnes et al., 2014), but the negative effect of biodiversity loss on soil functions may be at least in part counteracted by earthworms that monopolize the detrital channel in plantations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Earthworms may counteract the destabilization of the system through sequestration of carbon in their large body and thus strengthening 'slow' energy channeling.
source: Thereby, earthworms also may counteract the destabilization of the system through sequestration of carbon in their large body and thus strengthening 'slow' energy channeling (Rooney and McCann, 2012; Schwarzmüller et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings, supported by citations.

claim: High Δ13C values and shift in dominance of detritivore taxa suggest that the detrital energy channel in rainforest is diversified and comprises a wider range of consumer groups than in plantations.
source: Combined, high Δ13C values and shift in dominance of detritivore taxa suggest that the detrital energy channel in rainforest is diversified and comprises a wider range of consumer groups than in plantations, whereas in plantations it comprises almost exclusively Annelida.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The similar weighted average Δ13C values in plantations and rainforest suggest that from an energetic perspective, soil food webs in plantations are as efficient in processing old organic carbon as in rainforest.
source: The similar weighted average Δ13C values in plantations and rainforest suggest that from an energetic perspective, soil food webs in plantations are as efficient in processing old organic carbon as in rainforest, despite having a very different structure.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The decomposer system in plantations may be more vulnerable against future changes since their functioning relies on a single detritivore group comprising predominantly a single invasive species.
source: However, the decomposer system in plantations may be more vulnerable against future changes since their functioning relies on a single detritivore group comprising predominantly a single invasive species (Potapov et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings, supported by a citation.

claim: Lower Δ15N values in Oribatida and Blattodea in rainforest compared to plantations may be linked to their trophic plasticity.
source: Lower Δ15N values in Oribatida and Blattodea in rainforest compared to plantations may be linked to their trophic plasticity, allowing them to shift their trophic position from primary decomposer in rainforest to secondary decomposer in litter-poor plantations (Krause et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings, supported by a citation.

claim: The low Δ15N values in many taxa in oil palm may be due to feeding on resources depleted in Δ15N relative to litter, such as algae and lichens.
source: The low Δ15N values in these taxa at least in part may be due to feeding on resources depleted in Δ15N relative to litter, such as algae and lichens (Chahartaghi et al., 2005; Schneider et al., 2004), suggesting that non-vascular plants may play a more important role for groups such as Hemiptera, Orthoptera, and Isoptera in plantations than in rainforest, potentially associated with the more open canopies in plantations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings, supported by citations.

claim: The range of Δ15N values in soil communities reflects the length of food chains.
source: The range of Δ15N values in soil communities reflects the length of food chains (Cabana and Rasmussen, 1994; Scheu and Falca, 2000), and was the largest in jungle rubber.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Jungle rubber is a system that is highly heterogeneous in management practices and plant richness.
source: Jungle rubber is a system that is highly heterogeneous in management practices and plant richness (Gouyon et al., 1993; Rembold et al., 2017b), with species richness in some arthropod predators even exceeding that in rainforest at our study sites (Junggebauer et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Food chains have been found to be longest at intermediate levels of disturbance.
source: Anthropogenic disturbances in jungle rubber are moderate compared to monoculture plantation systems (Barnes et al., 2014) and food chains have been found to be longest at intermediate levels of disturbance (Menge and Sutherland, 1987; Polis and Winemiller, 2018; Post, 2002b), which may explain the largest range of Δ15N values in jungle rubber.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neither isotopic diversity nor isotopic redundancy were higher in rainforest than in plantations.
source: Refuting our second hypothesis, neither isotopic diversity nor isotopic redundancy were higher in rainforest than in plantations.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis that refutes a hypothesis.

claim: Isotopic richness was slightly higher in the two more natural systems (i.e., rainforest and jungle rubber) than in rubber and oil palm plantations.
source: However, isotopic richness was slightly higher in the two more natural systems (i.e., rainforest and jungle rubber) than in rubber and oil palm plantations.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Oil palm showed significantly higher community dispersion values than the other land-use systems.
source: Oil palm showed significantly higher community dispersion values than the other land-use systems and in trend had the highest community divergence (unweighted values) reflecting the proportion of groups with the most extreme trophic (isotopic) niches within the community (Cucherousset and Villéger, 2015; Mason et al., 2005; Villéger et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: The high dispersion and divergence in oil palm is at least in part due to feeding on non-vascular plants, such as algae and lichens.
source: At least in part this likely was due to feeding on non-vascular plants, such as algae and lichens, characterized by very different stable isotope values than C3 plants, that is, the dominant vegetation at our study sites (Potapov et al., 2019c).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings, supported by a citation.

claim: The more open canopy in plantations favors algae and lichens.
source: As discussed above, the more open canopy in plantations favors algae and lichens (Drescher et al., 2016; Schulz et al., 2019), together with the monopolization of detrital channel by earthworms (representing another 'extreme' isotopic niche), the use of non-vascular plants explains the high dispersion and divergence of energy channeling in oil palm plantations.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Food-web divergence in plantations was significantly higher than in rainforest from the 'energetic perspective'.
source: From the 'energetic perspective', soil food-web divergence in plantations was significantly higher than in rainforest.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Functional divergence decreases with disturbance according to previous evidence.
source: This contrasts previous evidence that functional divergence decreases with disturbance (Gerisch et al., 2012; Mouillot et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Energetic dispersion was in trend higher in rainforest than in the other land-use systems.
source: However, contrary to divergence, energetic dispersion was in trend higher in rainforest than in the other land-use systems.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Food webs in plantations are less balanced (low dispersion) with most of the energy being channeled and locked into earthworms.
source: Similar to the community metrics, the energetic metrics indicated that food-web characteristics in plantations deviate from those in rainforest (high divergence), with food webs being less balanced (low dispersion) with most of the energy being channeled and locked into earthworms.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Community isotopic uniqueness and community evenness were low in jungle rubber.
source: Community isotopic uniqueness, defined as the inverse of the average isotopic redundancy, and community evenness (Cucherousset and Villéger, 2015) were low in jungle rubber.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: High functional redundancy may buffer against land-use impacts and promote stable food webs with long trophic chains.
source: High functional redundancy may buffer against land-use impacts and promote stable food webs with long trophic chains (Brodie et al., 2014; Chua et al., 2021; Sanders et al., 2018), which is supported by the results of our study.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research and the study's findings.

claim: The increase in isotopic uniqueness in oil palm plantations may reflect eroded resilience of this system against future changes.
source: The increase in isotopic uniqueness (both energetic and unweighted) in oil palm plantations may reflect eroded resilience of this system against future changes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Community food-web metrics were more sensitive to changes in land use than energetic food-web metrics.
source: Overall, community food-web metrics were more sensitive to changes in land use than energetic food-web metrics, suggesting that compositional changes in soil food webs with land use are stronger than changes in energy channeling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Land-use effects on soil animal biodiversity exceed those on functional diversity.
source: This echoes earlier findings that land-use effects on soil animal biodiversity exceed those on functional diversity (Potapov et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: SEM indicated significant direct effects of land use-induced environmental changes on community food-web metrics.
source: Results of our SEM indicated significant direct effects of land use-induced environmental changes (i.e., litter amount, tree density, and tree species richness) on community food-web metrics.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's structural equation modeling.

claim: The amount and quality of leaf litter are important drivers of soil fauna composition and soil food-web structure.
source: The amount and quality of leaf litter are important drivers of soil fauna composition and soil food-web structure, being both the food and the habitat for soil animals (Fujii et al., 2020; Sayer et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Changes in tree density and species richness are associated with changes in root-derived resources.
source: Apart from litter-mediated effects, changes in tree density and species richness are associated with changes in root-derived resources (Ballauff et al., 2021), which also fuel belowground food webs (Pollierer et al., 2007; Bradford, 2016), and this may explain the direct effects of tree communities on the food-web metrics.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Energetic food-web metrics were not directly affected by changes in tree communities and pH, but were linked to the changes in earthworm abundance.
source: By contrast, energetic food-web metrics were not directly affected by changes in tree communities and pH, but were linked to the changes in earthworm abundance.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's structural equation modeling.

claim: High soil pH favors colonization of plantations by earthworms and this is common in the tropics.
source: High soil pH favors colonization of plantations by earthworms and this is common in the tropics (Marichal et al., 2010; Potapov et al., 2021b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The study is among the first comprehensive assessment of tropical soil food webs and their variation due to land-use changes.
source: In conclusion, our study is among the first comprehensive assessment of tropical soil food webs and their variation due to land-use changes.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty and contribution of the study.

claim: Low Δ13C values in most soil animal groups in plantations indicate a shift toward using plant carbon and 'fast' energy channeling.
source: Low Δ13C values in most soil animal groups in plantations in comparison to rainforest indicate a shift toward using plant carbon and 'fast' energy channeling based on high-quality understory plants (weeds) as well as algae.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The trophic niche of earthworms as major macrofauna detritivores stayed unchanged and they monopolized the 'slow' detrital channel in plantations.
source: On the other hand, the trophic niche of earthworms as major macrofauna detritivores stayed unchanged and they monopolized the 'slow' detrital channel in plantations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Changes in soil food-web characteristics with transformation of rainforest into plantations are associated with reduced soil functioning.
source: Other studies at our sites showed that these changes in soil food-web characteristics with transformation of rainforest into plantations are associated with reduced soil functioning (Grass et al., 2020) and litter invertebrate biodiversity (Barnes et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research at the same sites.

claim: Land-use effects on soil biodiversity from a 'community perspective' are in part buffered from the perspective of energy channeling ('energetic perspective').
source: Our analyses allowed to uncover the mechanisms responsible for these changes and demonstrated that land-use effects on soil biodiversity from a 'community perspective' are in part buffered from the perspective of energy channeling ('energetic perspective'), but resistance of plantations against future changes in climate and land use may be compromised.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Resistance of plantations against future changes in climate and land use may be compromised.
source: Our analyses allowed to uncover the mechanisms responsible for these changes and demonstrated that land-use effects on soil biodiversity from a 'community perspective' are in part buffered from the perspective of energy channeling ('energetic perspective'), but resistance of plantations against future changes in climate and land use may be compromised.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: Four land-use systems were investigated: rainforest, jungle rubber, rubber plantations, and oil palm plantations.
source: Four land-use systems, rainforest, jungle rubber, rubber plantations, and oil palm plantations were investigated in two regions, that is, Harapan and Bukit Duabelas (Drescher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study design.

claim: Each land-use system was replicated four times in each landscape, resulting in a total of 32 sites.
source: Each land-use system was replicated four times in each landscape, resulting in a total of 32 sites; for more details, see Drescher et al., 2016.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study design.

claim: Soil animals were sampled at each of 32 study sites during October and November 2013.
source: Soil animals were sampled at each of 32 study sites during October and November 2013.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study methodology.

claim: Animals were classified into 23 high-rank taxonomic groups.
source: Animals were classified into 23 high-rank taxonomic groups (Oribatida, Collembola, Symphyla, Protura, Annelida, Blattodea, Diplopoda, Isopoda, Isoptera, Psocoptera, Psocoptera, Lepidoptera, Orthoptera, Thysanoptera, Diptera, Coleoptera, Pseudoscorpiones, Mesostigmata, Diplura, Formicidae, Chilopoda, Araneae, Pauropoda).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study methodology.

claim: In total, 626 samples of 23 taxonomic groups were analyzed across 32 sites.
source: In total, 626 samples of 23 taxonomic groups were analyzed across 32 sites.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study data.

claim: The number of analyzed taxonomic groups varied between 6 and 17 per site and was on average 12.3.
source: The number of analyzed taxonomic groups varied between 6 and 17 per site (i.e., per one soil food web) and was on average 12.3.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study data.

claim: The 15N/14N isotope ratio is used to indicate the trophic position of species.
source: The 15N/14N isotope ratio is used to indicate the trophic position of species since it is enriched by about 3–4‰ per trophic level (Post, 2002a; Pollierer et al., 2009; Potapov et al., 2019c); 13C typically is little affected by trophic transfer and thus reflects basal food resources of the trophic chain (Peterson and Fry, 1987; Potapov et al., 2019c).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research and represents established knowledge in stable isotope ecology.
